newsitem.title: USA: Westinghouse loss seen as no surprise.
newsitem.headline: Westinghouse loss seen as no surprise.

text.p: Westinghouse Electric Corp on Tuesday posted a fourth-quarter loss of $34 million but analysts just shrugged, saying the company is still restructuring and they expect profit growth once it splits into two separate companies.

"I don't see any big surprises (in the earnings,") said Greg Drahuschak at Janney Montgomery Scott. "This company is still in the process of evolution. If you would characterize it in terms of life cycle, they're in early adolesence, not maturity."

Restructuring costs ate away at fourth-quarter results. Westinghouse posted a net loss of $34 million, or $0.08 per share, compared with a loss of $7 million, or $0.02 per share, in the year-ago quarter.
"The restructuring costs are not ongoing, fundamental costs," said Frank Bodenchak at Morgan Stanley. "I think we're seeing that the growth is beginning to come."

The 1996 fourth quarter included an after-tax loss of $91 million for the company's restructuring plan. Wall Street's consensus estimate for the quarter was a profit of $0.11 per share but the range was wide, with eight analysts estimating earnings from $0.05 to $0.20 per share, according to First Call.
Revenues rose to $2.45 billion from $1.9 billion.
Westinghouse plans to split its industrial and media businesses later this year into separate companies. The company late last year also announced workforce reductions in its industrial operations.
Analysts said they anticipate strong profit growth for the company's television and radio operations after the separation.

Bodenchak said radio operations already are growing revenues by 15 percent, above the industry average of 8 percent. In the fourth quarter, radio posted a 37 percent rise in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization on a 10 percent rise in sales.

Commenting on CBS, which Westinghouse acquired in November 1995, he said: "The network is coming off a difficult 1996 but they'll have the wind at their back in 1997. I expect significant incremental profit growth from syndication."
He said he expects two popular CBS shows, "Dr. Quinn Medicine Woman" and "Walker Texas Ranger," to bring the network $170 million this year.
Earnings at CBS fell in the quarter and full year, on a pro forma basis, due to lower demographic ratings and increased costs associated with political coverage and sports rights.
Bodenchak noted he initiated coverage of Westinghouse on Tuesday with an outperform rating, citing expected growth in media. The rating formerly had been neutral.
"I'm looking for (a stock price target) of $20 to $22 in '97 and $25 in '98," he said.
Westinghouse shares were up 5/8 to 18 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
For the year, Westinghouse posted net income of $30 million, or $0.07 per share. The company posted a loss of $0.05 per share in 1995 after dividends were paid on preferred stock.

Westinghouse's industrial group -- Thermo King, energy systems, power generation and government operations -- posted an 18 percent rise in operating profiton an 8 percent rise in sales in the fourth quarter.

Drahuschak said how well the industrial operations perform will depend on cyclical market conditions, some of which are out of the company's control. "You tell me what will happen in power generation, nuclear power support...anyone who makes a guess at that is taking a stab in the dark.
"Let's wait for the evolution process to be complete, see what this company is going to be."
